name: Carpal tunnel syndrome
aka: median nerve compression at the wrist
populations: people in forceful, repetitive or vibratory manual work
people with diabetes, obesity or thyroid disease
summary: Compression of the median nerve in the carpal tunnel, causing night-time pain, numbness and tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers and, in severe cases, thenar weakness. Most start with non-surgical care.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Symptoms are reviewed over weeks to 3 months with non-surgical care; surgery is considered when symptoms persist [Cochrane]

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No single test is reliable: pooled Phalen Sn 0.57, Sp 0.67; Tinel Sn 0.45, Sp 0.78. Combine history, hand diagram and sensorimotor tests

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Nerve conduction studies (median across the wrist versus a comparison nerve segment) are the most sensitive and accurate neurophysiological test

keyFacts.label: Outcome measure
keyFacts.value: Boston Carpal Tunnel Questionnaire (symptom and function scales, 1 = best, 5 = worst)

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Trial participants were mostly middle-aged women (84% women in the surgical-versus-non-surgical Cochrane trials)

keyFacts.label: Work link
keyFacts.value: Force, repetition and vibration are associated with CTS; evidence that computer work causes it is insufficient

overview:
Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) is a compression neuropathy of the median nerve at the wrist [r8]. It is the most common entrapment neuropathy [r2]. People typically report pain, numbness and tingling in the median nerve distribution, and some develop weakness, loss of dexterity and thenar wasting. An evidence-based physical therapy clinical practice guideline exists for CTS [r1]. Its individual recommendation grades were not retrievable for this page, so the treatment evidence below is taken from Cochrane reviews and randomised trials.

The pathophysiology is not fully understood, but mechanical compression with raised carpal tunnel pressure is the most likely mechanism, with ischaemia and demyelination of the nerve following [r3]. Work-related causation is contested. High hand force, repetitive work and vibration show consistent associations in a systematic review [r4], while evidence that computer work causes CTS is insufficient [r5]. Management follows a stepped pathway: education, activity modification and night splinting for milder symptoms, corticosteroid injection for short-term relief, and surgical release when symptoms persist or the nerve is failing [r8,r10,r11].

epidemiology.text:
CTS is the most common entrapment neuropathy; ulnar neuropathy at the elbow is the second most common [r2]. Population prevalence and incidence figures were not available in the sources retrieved for this page, so none are quoted. The people recruited into trials give a picture of who presents for treatment: in the 14 randomised trials in the Cochrane review of surgery versus non-surgical care, 84% of the 1231 participants were women and mean age ranged from 32 to 53 years [r8]. In 29 splinting trials of 1937 adults, mean age ranged from 42 to 60 years and mean symptom duration from seven weeks to five years [r9].

Occupational links exist but are not uniform across jobs and exposures. A systematic review found the highest risk of CTS in meat- and fish-processing work, forestry work with chainsaws and electronic assembly work (odds ratios 76.5, 21.3 and 11.4), and consistent indications of an association with hand-arm vibration, prolonged work with a flexed or extended wrist, high hand force and high repetitiveness [r4]. It found no association with psychosocial work factors and contradictory findings for computer work [r4]. A separate systematic review of eight studies concluded that there is insufficient epidemiological evidence that computer work causes CTS, although carpal tunnel pressure rose to potentially harmful levels during actual mouse use in one study [r5].

intrinsic: Female sex: 84% of participants in the surgical-versus-non-surgical trials were women [r8]
Middle age: mean ages in trials were about 32–60 years [r8,r9]

Systemic conditions commonly associated with CTS (diabetes, hypothyroidism, inflammatory arthritis, pregnancy, obesity); these associations are recognised clinically but were not quantified in the sources retrieved here
Wrist fracture or other trauma that reduces tunnel volume or causes swelling (see red flags for acute CTS)
extrinsic: Hand-arm vibration, high hand force (average requirement above 4 kg) and high repetitiveness [r4]
Prolonged work with a flexed or extended wrist [r4]
Meat- and fish-processing, chainsaw forestry and electronic assembly work have the highest reported odds ratios [r4]
Computer keyboard and mouse use: association unproven (insufficient evidence) [r5]

mechanism.summary: CTS has no single injury moment. Carpal tunnel pressure rises when the tunnel contents (nerve, flexor tendons and their synovial lining) outgrow the space available or when sustained wrist postures and loading increase the pressure on them. The median nerve is then compressed against the tough flexor retinaculum, which forms the roof of the tunnel [r3]. Elevated pressure, ischaemia, mechanical trauma, demyelination and tenosynovial change are all proposed contributors, with mechanical factors considered most likely [r3].
sequence: The wrist is held in sustained flexion or extension, or the hand grips forcefully and repeatedly (or is exposed to vibration), loading the flexor tendons within the carpal tunnel [r4].
Tunnel pressure rises. In one study, pressure during real mouse use rose to levels considered potentially harmful, although pressures in typical computer-user postures were below those levels [r5].
The median nerve, the softest structure in the tunnel, is squeezed between the tendons and the flexor retinaculum [r3].
Nerve blood flow falls (ischaemia) [r3]. Symptoms typically appear first at night or with sustained wrist postures and ease when the hand is shaken or the wrist is moved (clinical presentation).
With continued compression, myelin is damaged (demyelination) and conduction slows, which is detectable on nerve conduction studies [r3].
In prolonged severe compression, axons can be lost: sensation becomes constant, thumb abduction weakens and the thenar muscles waste.

Release of the retinaculum (surgery) or offloading of the tunnel (splint, injection, activity change) lowers pressure and allows the nerve to recover, but nerve recovery is slower when axonal loss is present.

variants.name: Occupational and repetitive-use pattern
variants.description: Forceful, repetitive and vibratory hand work shows consistent associations with CTS, but causation in an individual remains difficult to prove [r4].

variants.name: Computer and keyboard use
variants.description: Epidemiological evidence that computer work causes CTS is insufficient; do not assume desk work is the cause without ruling out other contributors [r5].

variants.name: Systemic or fluid-retention pattern
variants.description: Pregnancy, diabetes, thyroid disease and inflammatory arthritis are commonly associated with CTS, often bilateral, and tend to need medical review as well as local management (clinical association; not quantified in the sources retrieved).

variants.name: Acute traumatic CTS
variants.description: After distal radius fracture or wrist dislocation, swelling, haematoma or displaced bone can raise tunnel pressure rapidly. This is a surgical emergency and is covered under red flags.

anatomy.text: The carpal tunnel is a fibro-osseous passage on the palmar side of the wrist. Its floor and sides are formed by the arched carpal bones, and its roof is the flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament). It carries the digital flexor tendons and the median nerve, which lies directly under the retinaculum. The median nerve gives sensation to the palmar thumb, index, middle and radial half of the ring finger, and its recurrent motor branch supplies the thenar muscles. The palmar cutaneous branch leaves the nerve before the tunnel, so thenar-eminence sensation is typically spared in CTS and helps separate CTS from more proximal median nerve lesions (clinical anatomy).

structures.name: Median nerve
structures.role: Sensory to the palmar thumb, index, middle and half of the ring finger; motor to the thenar muscles via the recurrent branch

structures.name: Flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament)
structures.role: Forms the roof of the tunnel and holds the flexor tendons against the carpus. It is the structure divided in carpal tunnel release

structures.name: Digital flexor tendons and synovial sheaths
structures.role: Flex the fingers; their synovial lining shares the tunnel with the nerve and can thicken or swell

structures.name: Carpal bones (tunnel floor and walls)
structures.role: Rigid arch that makes the tunnel a fixed-volume space, so small volume changes alter pressure

structures.name: Thenar muscles
structures.role: Abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis and part of flexor pollicis brevis produce thumb abduction and opposition; they weaken and waste when the motor fibres fail

structures.name: Palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve
structures.role: Arises proximal to the tunnel and supplies the thenar eminence skin, so that area is normally spared in CTS

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
The median nerve is injured by compression within a space that cannot expand. The sources describe several contributing processes: elevated carpal tunnel pressure, ischaemia, mechanical trauma, ectopic impulse generation, demyelination, tenosynovial change and involvement of both small and large fibres, with mechanical aspects considered the most likely cause [r3]. Early on the changes are reversible, so symptoms come and go and settle when the pressure is relieved.

If compression persists, the myelin sheath is damaged and conduction through the wrist slows, which is why nerve conduction studies comparing the median segment across the wrist with another nerve segment are the most sensitive and accurate neurophysiological tests [r3]. In long-standing severe compression, axons can degenerate. Axonal loss recovers more slowly and less completely, which is the rationale for earlier surgery when there is constant numbness, thenar weakness or wasting. The randomised trial of surgery versus non-surgical care specifically studied people without denervation, so its results do not apply to people with established axonal loss [r11].

structures.name: Median nerve
structures.effect: Intraneural oedema, ischaemia and focal demyelination at the tunnel inlet; in severe long-standing cases, axonal loss [r3]

structures.name: Flexor retinaculum
structures.effect: Fixed roof of the tunnel. It does not stretch, so any increase in contents raises pressure; division of the ligament decompresses the tunnel (clinical anatomy)

structures.name: Flexor tendons and tenosynovium
structures.effect: Tenosynovial thickening or swelling can reduce space for the nerve; tendonitis is listed among proposed contributors [r3]

structures.name: Thenar muscles
structures.effect: Weakness and wasting of abductor pollicis brevis and opponens pollicis when motor fibres are affected (clinical anatomy)

structures.name: Skin and sensory receptors
structures.effect: Reduced sensation, and objective tests such as two-point discrimination and monofilaments are subjective and less sensitive than nerve conduction studies [r3]

muscles.name: Abductor pollicis brevis and opponens pollicis
muscles.effect: Weakness of thumb abduction and opposition, then wasting if axons are lost (clinical anatomy).

muscles.name: Flexor tendon-driven grip muscles
muscles.effect: Grip is reduced by pain, paraesthesia and loss of dexterity. Patients drop objects and avoid fine tasks, which leads to disuse (clinical observation).

muscles.name: Forearm and shoulder girdle muscles
muscles.effect: Compensatory guarding of the arm and neck can accompany long-standing symptoms; examine the cervical spine and proximal arm for contributors (clinical observation).

cellular.timing: Intermittent, during sustained postures or night
cellular.description: Raised tunnel pressure compresses the nerve. Venous congestion and intraneural oedema then reduce its blood flow (standard nerve-compression biology). Elevated carpal tunnel pressure and ischaemia are the proposed drivers [r3].
Ischaemia and involvement of both small and large fibres produce intermittent paraesthesia that eases when pressure is relieved [r3].

cellular.timing: Weeks to months of persistent compression
cellular.description: Focal myelin damage slows conduction through the wrist, detectable as prolonged latencies on nerve conduction studies [r3].

cellular.timing: Months to years in severe cases
cellular.description: Axons are lost distal to the lesion, producing constant numbness, weakness and thenar wasting (basic nerve biology).
Axons regrow from the site of injury at a slow rate. Recovery is better in nerves with demyelination alone than in those with axonal loss (basic nerve biology; the rate is not quoted here).

systems.effect: Ectopic impulse generation and involvement of small and large fibres explain the mix of pain, paraesthesia and numbness [r3]. Central sensitisation may maintain symptoms in long-standing cases (plausible, not established in the sources retrieved).
Ischaemia of the nerve is one of the proposed mechanisms [r3]; venous congestion in the tunnel is the usual explanation for how pressure reduces nerve blood flow.
Cervical spine, thoracic outlet and elbow can contribute to arm symptoms (double-crush concept). Screen the neck and proximal nerve path for competing causes.
Diabetes, thyroid disease and pregnancy are commonly associated with CTS. Ask about them, because treating the underlying condition may change the management plan (clinical association).
Prognostic factors for return to work after surgery include lower recovery expectations, worse mental health, high job strain, workers' compensation status and attorney involvement [r15].

grading.system: Practical severity grouping (clinical convention, not a validated cut-off set)

grades.description: Intermittent night-time or activity-related paraesthesia, normal sensation and strength between episodes. Nerve conduction studies are normal or show mild slowing.
grades.prognosis: Often managed with education, activity modification and a night splint, then reviewed [r9]

grades.description: Frequent or persistent symptoms, reduced dexterity, objective sensory change in the median distribution. Slowed conduction is usual.
grades.prognosis: Splint, injection or surgery can be considered; injection benefit is short term [r10]; surgery reduces later surgery referral compared with splinting [r8]

grades.description: Constant numbness, thenar weakness or wasting, absent sensation, or a denervation pattern on electrodiagnostic testing.
grades.prognosis: Early surgical referral is usual. The key trial excluded people with denervation, so its findings do not apply to this group [r11]

timeframes.summary: CTS has no fixed healing timeline: it follows nerve compression biology, and it responds to load management and offloading. The phases below are illustrative of nerve biology and are not drawn from a single cited source. Treatment effects from trials are reported at about 1 month for injection [r10] and at more than 3 months for surgery versus splinting [r8].

healing.description: Venous congestion and ischaemia produce night and activity-related symptoms that settle when pressure is relieved [r3]
Focal myelin damage and slowed conduction; symptoms become more frequent and function declines [r3]

healing.phase: Axonal loss in severe long-standing compression
healing.description: Constant numbness and thenar weakness; slower and less complete recovery (illustrative, basic nerve biology)
Night symptoms often settle first, with sensation and strength recovering over months (clinical experience; varies widely)

milestones.label: Review response to night splint and activity change
milestones.note: A 6-week trial is a common clinical convention; splinting evidence is low certainty [r9]

milestones.label: Injection effect expected
milestones.note: Short-term benefit at one month or less was shown against placebo; relief beyond one month was not demonstrated [r10]

milestones.label: Decision point for surgery
milestones.note: Cochrane trials compare surgery with non-surgical care at more than 3 months [r8]

milestones.label: Return to light hand use after release
milestones.note: Typical surgeon-directed convention; follow the operating surgeon's protocol

milestones.label: Return to full manual work after release
milestones.note: Varies with job demands; workers' compensation status and recovery expectations influence return to work [r15]

timeframes.returnToSport: Not sport-specific; return to work and activity is criteria-based. Light use is usually allowed within days to weeks after release, and full manual duties commonly take about 4–8 weeks, depending on the job and the surgeon's protocol (a common clinical convention). Recovery of grip and sensation can take months.

symptoms: Numbness, tingling or burning in the thumb, index, middle and radial ring finger
Night-time waking with a painful, numb hand that eases when the hand is shaken or the wrist moved
Symptoms provoked by sustained gripping, driving, phone use or other prolonged wrist postures
Clumsiness and dropping objects; difficulty with buttons or fine tasks
Pain in the wrist or forearm, sometimes radiating up the arm, in many people
signs: Reduced light-touch or pinprick sensation in the median distribution, often sparing the thenar eminence
Positive provocation: Phalen test, Tinel sign or carpal compression test (individually unreliable [r6])
Thumb abduction weakness (abductor pollicis brevis) in more advanced cases
Thenar wasting in severe, long-standing compression
Normal neck range and normal reflexes if CTS is the sole problem

subjective: Distribution of symptoms (use a hand diagram), relation to night, sustained postures and work or hobby tasks
Onset, duration, one or both hands, and whether symptoms are progressing or constant
Previous wrist fracture or trauma, ongoing swelling, and for acute onset after trauma, how quickly the symptoms developed
Medical history: diabetes, thyroid disease, inflammatory arthritis, pregnancy, renal disease, amyloid
Occupational and hobby exposure to force, repetition, vibration and sustained wrist postures
Neck, shoulder and elbow symptoms that suggest a proximal or double-crush contribution
Boston Carpal Tunnel Questionnaire at baseline to track change [r7]
observation: Skin changes, swelling, scars or deformity from previous fracture
Posture of the wrist and neck during tasks such as typing or tool use
palpation: Tenderness over the tunnel and proximal median nerve
Swelling or mass in the palm or wrist crease
rangeOfMotion: Active wrist flexion and extension, comparing sides (note symptom provocation at end range)
Cervical and shoulder screen to exclude a proximal cause
strength: Thumb abduction against resistance (abductor pollicis brevis)
Grip dynamometry compared with the other side and norms
neuro: Light-touch and pinprick sensation in the median, ulnar and radial distributions; check for thenar sparing
Two-point discrimination or monofilament testing (more subjective and less sensitive than nerve conduction studies [r3])
Reflexes and upper-limb neurological screen for cervical radiculopathy or myelopathy
Median nerve neurodynamic testing as a provocation and mobility measure (no accuracy figures quoted)
functional: Observe typing, tool use or grip tasks
Timed functional tasks (button, pick up small objects) or patient-specific functional scale

specialTests.name: Phalen test
specialTests.purpose: Provoke median nerve symptoms with wrist flexion
specialTests.procedure: The patient holds the wrists in full flexion, backs of the hands together, for up to 60 seconds (a common time convention).
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of tingling or numbness in the median distribution.

specialTests.name: Tinel sign
specialTests.purpose: Detect an irritable median nerve at the carpal tunnel
specialTests.procedure: Tap lightly over the median nerve at the wrist crease, from proximal to distal.
specialTests.positive: Tingling in the median nerve distribution.

specialTests.name: Carpal compression test (Durkan)
specialTests.purpose: Provoke symptoms by direct pressure over the tunnel
specialTests.procedure: Apply firm thumb pressure over the carpal tunnel for about 30 seconds (common convention).

specialTests.name: Hand diagram and sensorimotor testing
specialTests.purpose: Pattern recognition for median-distribution symptoms plus objective sensory and motor loss
specialTests.procedure: Patient shades the symptom area on a hand diagram; examine sensation by dermatome and the strength of thumb abduction.
specialTests.positive: Symptoms in the palmar thumb and first three fingers with thenar sparing, plus sensory or motor change. The meta-analysis authors recommend combining provocative tests with sensorimotor tests, hand diagrams and questionnaires rather than relying on one test [r6].

clinicalRules.name: Combine findings rather than rely on a single test
clinicalRules.description: In a meta-analysis of 31 studies of 12 provocative maneuvers, no single test was reliable enough. The authors advised combining provocative tests with sensorimotor tests, hand diagrams and diagnostic questionnaires [r6].

outcomeMeasures.name: Boston Carpal Tunnel Questionnaire (BCTQ): Symptom Severity and Functional Status scales
outcomeMeasures.use: Condition-specific, reproducible and responsive to change; scored 1 (best) to 5 (worst) [r7]. Cochrane reviews use MCIDs of 1 point for symptoms and 0.7 for function [r8].

outcomeMeasures.name: QuickDASH or PRWE
outcomeMeasures.use: Region-specific upper-limb function; track change across rehabilitation (no cut-offs quoted)

outcomeMeasures.name: Grip and pinch dynamometry
outcomeMeasures.use: Objective strength, compared with the other side

outcomeMeasures.name: Night-waking and pain numeric rating
outcomeMeasures.use: Simple tracking of the patient's priority symptoms

imaging.modality: Nerve conduction studies (with EMG when indicated)
imaging.indication: Confirm the diagnosis when doubt exists, plan surgery, assess severity or look for other neuropathy
imaging.findings: Slowed median sensory or motor conduction across the wrist compared with another nerve segment; this comparison is the most sensitive and accurate neurophysiological approach [r3]. Denervation changes on EMG suggest axonal loss.

imaging.indication: Adjunct to visualise the nerve and exclude a mass or anatomical variant
imaging.findings: Median nerve enlargement at the tunnel inlet (no accuracy figures quoted here)

imaging.indication: Previous trauma, arthritis or suspected fracture
imaging.findings: Malunited distal radius, carpal arthritis or other bony causes of reduced tunnel space

differentials.name: Cervical radiculopathy (C6–C7)
differentials.distinguishing: Neck pain, symptoms provoked by neck movement (Spurling), dermatomal pattern including the dorsal hand or forearm, reflex change.

differentials.name: Thoracic outlet syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Whole-arm symptoms, ulnar side more affected, provoked by overhead positions and reproduced by neurovascular provocation.

differentials.name: Cubital tunnel syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Ring and little finger numbness, elbow flexion provocation, positive Tinel at the cubital tunnel.

differentials.name: Ulnar tunnel (Guyon's canal) syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Ulnar-distribution sensory or motor loss at the wrist, often after cycling or direct pressure.

differentials.name: De Quervain's tenosynovitis
differentials.distinguishing: Radial wrist pain at the first dorsal compartment, positive Finkelstein, no night paraesthesia in the median distribution.

differentials.name: Pronator teres syndrome or proximal median neuropathy
differentials.distinguishing: Forearm pain, symptoms in the palm (palmar cutaneous branch involved) and provocation by resisted pronation; thenar sensation is not spared.

differentials.name: Peripheral polyneuropathy (e.g. diabetic)
differentials.distinguishing: Symmetrical, glove-distribution sensory loss, often in the feet as well; investigate systemically.

differentials.name: Thumb carpometacarpal osteoarthritis
differentials.distinguishing: Pain at the thumb base with grind test and loss of key pinch; no night-time median paraesthesia unless coexisting CTS.

redFlags: Acute onset numbness and pain after a distal radius fracture, wrist dislocation or crush injury: suspect acute carpal tunnel syndrome. Elevate, release any tight dressing or cast, and arrange same-day emergency surgical review for decompression.

Severe or increasing pain out of proportion, pain on passive finger stretch, tense swelling or pallor in the forearm or hand: suspect compartment syndrome or vascular compromise. Refer to emergency immediately.
Constant numbness, thenar wasting or progressive thumb weakness: nerve damage is established. Refer urgently to hand surgery for nerve conduction studies and consideration of release.
Hot, red, swollen palm or finger with fever, or a wound near the wrist: suspect infection such as flexor tenosynovitis. Refer to emergency.
Symptoms in both arms with leg involvement, gait change or hyperreflexia: suspect cervical myelopathy. Refer urgently for imaging.

Bilateral symptoms with systemic features (weight change, fatigue, polyneuropathy, new inflammatory joint pain): arrange medical review for diabetes, thyroid disease, amyloid or inflammatory arthritis.

management.principles: Decisions are shared between the patient and clinician and follow severity, symptom pattern, work and preference. For mild to moderate symptoms, start with education, activity modification and a neutral night splint, add a corticosteroid injection if symptoms are limiting, and move to carpal tunnel release when symptoms persist, are severe, or there is sensory loss or weakness. Cochrane reviews rate much of the non-surgical evidence as low or very-low certainty [r9,r12], and say that patients with severe symptoms, a strong preference for improvement and reluctance to continue non-surgical care may choose surgery, whereas people with tolerable symptoms who want to avoid surgical morbidity can start non-surgically [r8,r9]. A physical therapy guideline for CTS exists [r1] but its grades were not retrievable, so no treatment is labelled here with a guideline recommendation strength.

medical.name: Carpal tunnel release (surgery)
medical.description: Division of the flexor retinaculum (open or endoscopic) to decompress the median nerve. Compared with splinting at more than 3 months, surgery probably gives a higher rate of clinical improvement (RR 2.10, 95% CI 1.04–4.24; moderate certainty) but probably does not give a clinically important improvement in BCTQ symptoms or function; it probably reduces further surgery (44% of the splinting group were referred to surgery versus none repeating surgery in the surgery group) [r8]. Against corticosteroid injection at more than 3 months, the difference in clinical improvement is uncertain [r8]. A 12-month trial found a statistically significant advantage for surgery in function and symptoms that the authors called modest in clinical terms [r11].

medical.name: Local corticosteroid injection
medical.description: Injected into or near the carpal tunnel by a doctor. In two high-quality trials (141 participants), clinical improvement at one month or less was greater than with placebo injection (RR 2.58, 95% CI 1.72–3.87). Significant relief beyond one month has not been demonstrated, local injection was better than oral steroid for up to 3 months, and two injections did not add benefit over one [r10]. In one study, 12 of 83 participants (15%) needed surgery after injection [r8].

medical.name: Oral corticosteroid
medical.description: A short oral course. In the Cochrane injection review, local injection gave more improvement than oral steroid at up to 3 months [r10]. Systemic side effects limit routine use.

medical.name: Treatment of associated conditions
medical.description: Optimise diabetes and thyroid disease, and review inflammatory arthritis and pregnancy-related causes. Symptoms of pregnancy-related CTS may settle after delivery (clinical experience).

physio.name: Education, pacing and activity modification
physio.description: Explain the condition and its good outlook with treatment, identify aggravating postures and tasks, adjust workstation and tool use, and plan micro-breaks. Because work-related causation evidence is mixed, focus on symptom triggers rather than assuming a work cause [r4,r5].

physio.name: Neutral wrist night splint
physio.description: A neutral-position splint worn at night (and for aggravating tasks) as a low-cost, low-risk trial. Against no active treatment, splinting may give little or no symptom benefit in the short term (BCTQ symptom scale 0.37 points better, 95% CI 0.82 better to 0.08 worse; low certainty). One study (80 participants) suggested night-time splinting may raise the chance of overall improvement (RR 3.86, 95% CI 2.29–6.51; low certainty). Adverse effects were transient [r9].

physio.name: Median nerve and tendon gliding exercises
physio.description: Gentle sliding exercises for the median nerve and the finger flexor tendons, performed without provoking symptoms. The Cochrane review found limited and very-low-quality evidence for diverse exercise and mobilisation interventions, so the decision should rest on clinician expertise and patient preference [r12].

physio.name: Manual therapy and carpal bone mobilisation
physio.description: Soft-tissue and carpal mobilisation as an adjunct. The evidence is limited and of very low quality, with small trials at high risk of bias [r12].

physio.name: Graded strengthening and return-to-task program
physio.description: After symptoms settle or after surgery, rebuild grip and wrist capacity and return to tasks gradually (see rehab stages). There is no trial evidence quoted here for a specific strengthening protocol.

physio.name: Low-level laser therapy
physio.description: Cochrane review of 22 trials (1153 participants) found very-low-quality evidence and no data to support any clinical effect over placebo [r13].

physio.name: Therapeutic ultrasound
physio.description: Cochrane review of 11 studies (414 participants) found only poor-quality evidence from very limited data, and no support for greater benefit than other non-surgical treatments [r14]. Prefer interventions with better support.

education: Carpal tunnel syndrome is a squeezed nerve at the wrist. Early symptoms are usually reversible with treatment, but long-standing severe compression can cause permanent numbness and weakness.
Night splints and activity changes are low-risk to try. Injections often help for weeks, not months, and surgery is an option when symptoms persist or the nerve is failing.
Shake or change the position of the hand when it goes numb, avoid sustained wrist bending and break up repetitive tasks, but be aware that work is only one of several possible contributors.
Tell your clinician urgently if you develop constant numbness, weakness of the thumb, or any numbness after a wrist injury.
Surgery reduces the chance of needing further surgery compared with splinting alone, and most people see benefit, though the average difference over non-surgical care is modest [r8,r11].

rehab.overview: Rehabilitation is symptom- and capacity-based. Stage 1 offloads the nerve and settles night symptoms; stage 2 restores mobility and nerve sliding; stage 3 rebuilds strength; stage 4 returns the person to full work and recreational tasks with load management. The stages apply to non-surgical care and, with the precautions listed, after carpal tunnel release (follow the surgeon's protocol). Exercise evidence is limited and of very low quality [r12], so dosages below are common clinical conventions, and the program is adjusted to symptom irritability rather than to time alone.

stages.name: Settle symptoms & offload the nerve
precautions: Do not provoke more than mild, short-lived tingling during exercises
After release, protect the wound and follow the surgeon's lifting and scar rules
Refer urgently if numbness becomes constant or weakness appears

exercises.name: Neutral wrist night splint
exercises.dosage: Every night for a 6-week trial (common clinical convention); also during aggravating tasks if helpful

exercises.name: Median nerve glide (slider)
exercises.cues: Move gently; stop if tingling lasts longer than a few minutes

exercises.name: Tendon gliding series
exercises.dosage: Five hand positions × 10 repetitions, 3–5 times daily
exercises.cues: Straight, hook, full fist, table-top and straight fist

exercises.name: Gentle active wrist flexion and extension
Activity pacing and micro-breaks
exercises.dosage: Change wrist and hand posture every 20–30 minutes during sustained tasks
exercises.cues: Keep the wrist near neutral and loosen the grip

progressionCriteria: Tolerates daily range-of-motion exercise with only mild, short-lived symptoms
No progressive motor loss or constant numbness

stages.name: Restore mobility & nerve sliding
goals: Improve nerve sliding without provoking symptoms
precautions: Avoid sustained end-range wrist flexion or extension
Introduce nerve tension (tensioner) work only if irritability is low

exercises.name: Median nerve slider progressing to gentle tensioner
exercises.cues: Slide the nerve; do not stretch it into numbness

exercises.name: Wrist flexor and extensor stretches (elbow straight)
Thumb abduction and opposition (putty or band)
exercises.cues: Lift the thumb away from the palm; make firm pinch to each fingertip

exercises.name: Light grip squeezes
exercises.dosage: 2 × 10 with a soft ball, 3–5 s holds

exercises.name: Keyboard and mouse set-up review
exercises.cues: Keep the forearm supported and the wrist close to neutral

progressionCriteria: Symptoms mild with usual daily activity
Night symptoms rarely wake the patient
Thumb abduction and opposition at least equal to the other side or pre-injury

stages.name: Strength & capacity
goals: Build forearm endurance for work tasks
Tolerate loaded wrist extension in weight-bearing positions
precautions: Progress load only if symptoms do not increase for the next 24 hours
After release, delay heavy gripping and weight-bearing through the palm until scar tenderness settles and the surgeon allows it

exercises.name: Wrist extension with dumbbell (forearm supported)
exercises.cues: Slow lowering; keep the elbow supported

exercises.name: Wrist flexion with dumbbell (forearm supported)
exercises.cues: Control the movement and avoid end-range flexion

exercises.name: Grip strengthening (putty, gripper or towel wring)
exercises.cues: Squeeze firmly while keeping the wrist in neutral

exercises.name: Incline or wall push-up (wrist loading progression)
exercises.dosage: 3 × 8–12 on an incline, progressing to floor if tolerated
exercises.cues: Wrists under shoulders; stop if tingling builds

progressionCriteria: Grip strength approaching the other side (a common target is at least 80–90%)
No increase in tingling after loading sessions
BCTQ symptom and function scores clearly improved from baseline [r7]
Tolerates sustained grip tasks for the required work time

stages.name: Return to full work & activity
goals: Return to usual work and recreation
Know early warning signs of recurrence
precautions: Avoid sudden jumps in hand-intensive hours
Re-refer if numbness becomes constant or weakness develops

exercises.name: Simulated work tasks (tool use, assembly, keyboard sets)
exercises.dosage: Graded exposure: start at 50% of usual duration and add about 10–20% per week (common convention)
exercises.cues: Alternate tasks and take planned micro-breaks

exercises.name: Keyboard and mouse tolerance build
exercises.dosage: Begin with 20–30 minutes blocks, progressing as symptoms allow

exercises.name: Heavy grip and wrist strength maintenance
Vibration and tool-handle strategies
exercises.cues: Use padded handles, reduce force, and schedule recovery between vibration exposures

progressionCriteria: Full usual duties completed without a flare
BCTQ scores stable near the best achieved [r7]
Patient understands pacing and warning signs
Return-to-work plan agreed with employer where needed

criteria: Night-time symptoms absent or rare, and no constant numbness
Grip and pinch strength at about 80–90% of the other side or the person's pre-injury level (a common convention)
Sensation and thumb abduction recovering or stable on repeat examination
Tolerates a full day of usual hand tasks without a symptom flare
Scar tender-free and wound healed if surgery was performed
BCTQ scores improved and stable, with the patient satisfied with function [r7]
tests: Semmes-Weinstein or two-point discrimination if sensory change persists

prognosis: Prognosis varies with severity and duration. Against no active treatment, splinting may give little short-term benefit and longer-term effects are uncertain [r9]. Injection gives relief in the short term, but relief beyond one month was not demonstrated in the Cochrane review [r10]. Compared with splinting at more than 3 months, surgery probably gives a higher rate of improvement and reduces later surgery: in the pooled studies, 44% of the splinting group were referred to surgery versus none needing repeat surgery in the surgery group, although symptom and function differences on the BCTQ were below the minimal clinically important difference [r8]. In one trial, surgery had a modest 12-month advantage over multimodal non-surgical care, and no clinically important adverse events or surgical complications were reported [r11]. After surgery, factors linked with slower or poorer return to work include older age, greater upper-extremity limitation, more than two musculoskeletal pain sites, lower recovery expectations, worse mental health, high job strain, workers' compensation status, attorney involvement and a longer wait for surgery [r15].
prevention: Reduce sustained end-range wrist postures and break up repetitive or forceful hand tasks (associations with high hand force, repetitiveness and vibration are consistent in a systematic review [r4]).
Reduce hand-arm vibration exposure and use well-fitting, padded tool handles where vibration is part of the job [r4].
Do not assume keyboard or mouse use causes CTS; evidence is insufficient, so focus on posture and breaks without over-attributing cause [r5].
Manage associated medical conditions (diabetes, thyroid disease, inflammatory arthritis) and review fluid-retention causes such as pregnancy.
clinicalPearls: No single provocative test rules CTS in or out: Tinel has higher specificity than sensitivity, and Phalen has only moderate values. Combine a hand diagram, sensory and motor testing and the pattern of night symptoms [r6].

Thenar eminence sensation is normally spared in CTS because the palmar cutaneous branch arises before the tunnel; sensory loss over the thenar eminence points to a more proximal median lesion or another diagnosis.
Nerve conduction studies are most useful when comparing median conduction across the wrist with another nerve segment; use them if the diagnosis is uncertain or surgery is planned [r3].
Check the neck, thoracic outlet and elbow in every patient with arm paraesthesia, because a proximal contribution changes the plan.
Be honest about work causation: forceful, repetitive and vibratory work is consistently associated, but the evidence for desk and computer work is inconclusive [r4,r5].
After wrist fracture, ask about new numbness at every visit. Rapid-onset median symptoms need same-day escalation.

forces.label: Sustained wrist extension and finger load

captions.text: A keyboard worker types for hours with the wrist held in extension.
Sustained wrist postures, force and repetition load the structures in the carpal tunnel.
Pressure in the tunnel rises and the median nerve is squeezed under the retinaculum.
Work links are mixed: force, repetition and vibration are supported; desk work is unproven.
Zooming into the right wrist, palm side.

actions.text: Carpal tunnel: rigid floor, ligament roof
Thenar wasting in severe, long-standing cases

captions.text: The tunnel has a bony floor and the flexor retinaculum as its roof.
The median nerve lies just under the retinaculum, beside the flexor tendons.
Tendon swelling or sustained postures raise the pressure in this fixed-volume space.
The nerve is compressed, its blood flow falls and it becomes irritable.
With persistent compression the nerve is constricted at the tunnel inlet.
If motor fibres fail, the thenar muscles weaken and waste.
Release of the retinaculum or offloading the tunnel lowers the pressure.
A healthy myelinated axon conducts signals quickly and has a good blood supply.
Raised tunnel pressure compresses the nerve and impedes its blood flow.
Ischaemia makes the nerve fire abnormally: tingling and numbness, worse at night.
Persistent pressure damages the myelin, so conduction through the wrist slows.
Severe compression injures the axons themselves.
Axons distal to the lesion degenerate (Wallerian degeneration) and muscles lose their supply.
After decompression, axons can regrow slowly, which is why early relief gives better recovery.
